title: Stateful failover, regions, RPO and RTO
summary: Stateless tiers fail over by routing; data does not. Synchronous standbys, promotion, split brain and fencing tokens; active-passive and active-active regions; DNS failover in practice; RPO and RTO in numbers.

steps.title: Stateless fails over by routing, state does not
body: A **stateless** app server holds nothing you cannot lose. When it dies the load balancer stops sending it
traffic and you are done. A **database** holds the only copy of recent writes, so failing it over is a
procedure:
```text
zone a                          zone b
[primary] ==sync replication==> [standby]
x  dies
1. detect   (several failed checks, 10-30 s)
2. fence    the old primary: it must never accept another write
3. promote  the standby to primary
4. repoint  clients (a floating endpoint or DNS name)
5. rebuild  a new standby from the new primary
Managed databases with a standby in another zone typically fail over in tens of seconds to a couple of
minutes. During that window writes fail, so clients need timeouts and retries.
- **Synchronous standby**: the primary waits for the standby to confirm each commit. No committed write is lost on failover, but every commit pays a cross-zone round trip (about 1 ms).
- **Asynchronous replica**: the primary does not wait. Commits are faster, but writes still in flight when the primary dies are lost.
- **Split brain**: two nodes both believe they are the primary and both accept writes. The data diverges and someone has to merge it by hand.

- **Fencing**: making sure the old primary cannot write after a new one is promoted: cut its network, power it off, or reject writes that carry an old **fencing token** (an epoch number that grows with every promotion).
Tools like Patroni avoid split brain by keeping the leader lock in a consensus store (etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper):
a primary that cannot renew its lease demotes itself.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a safe database failover in order.
lines: Detect that the primary is unhealthy (several failed checks in a row)
Fence the old primary so it cannot accept writes
Point clients at the new primary
Build a new standby from the new primary
steps.explain: Fencing comes before promotion: if the old primary is only slow, not dead, promoting first creates two primaries. Rebuilding the standby comes last, and until it is done you have no protection against a second failure.

prompt: **Symptom first.** After a 40-second network partition between zones, the orders table has 212 pairs of rows
with the same `order_id` but different contents, created in both zones during those 40 seconds. A home-made
failover script promotes the standby when it cannot reach the primary for 10 seconds. What went wrong?
options: Split brain: the old primary was never fenced, so both nodes accepted writes during the partition
The order ids were not random enough
The partition was too short to cause a failover
explain: "Cannot reach the primary" does not mean "the primary is down": it was alive on the other side of the
partition and kept taking writes. Without fencing (a lease in a consensus store, a fencing token checked on

steps.title: Multi-region: active-passive and active-active
body: Zones protect against a data centre failure. **Regions** protect against a whole regional outage or a
disaster, and bring the service closer to distant users. They cost much more, mostly in complexity.
| | Active-passive | Active-active |
| Traffic | all in region 1; region 2 waits | both regions serve users |
| Writes | one primary region; async replica in region 2 | writes in both regions |
| Failover | promote region 2, move traffic (minutes) | stop sending traffic to the bad region (seconds to minutes) |
| Data loss on failover | writes in the replication lag | depends on conflict handling |
| Hard part | keeping region 2 tested and big enough | conflicting writes to the same record (module 6) |
| Cost | pay for idle capacity, or scale up during failover | each region needs headroom for the other's traffic |
Cross-region replication is almost always **asynchronous**: a synchronous commit across 70-150 ms of
round trip would make every write slow. So a regional failover usually loses the last moments of writes.
Many teams keep data writes in one home region per user or per tenant ("partitioned active-active") so
each record has exactly one writer.

steps.prompt: Which multi-region design does each statement describe?
items: The second region is idle until a failover
Users are served by the nearest region all the time
Two users can update the same record in two regions at once
Failover means promoting a replica and moving all traffic
The standby region is easy to forget about until it is needed, so it must be tested
Each region must keep headroom for the other region's users

steps.title: RPO, RTO and DNS in practice
body: - **RPO** (recovery point objective): how much recent data you may lose, measured in time. With async replication, RPO is at least the replication lag.
- **RTO** (recovery time objective): how long until the service works again after a failure.
```text
writes lost  ~= write rate x replication lag at the moment of failure
= 1,200 writes/s x 2.5 s = 3,000 writes
RTO         ~= time to detect + time to promote + time for clients to move
**DNS failover is slower than its TTL suggests.** A health-checked DNS record switches to region 2, but:
- clients cache the old answer for up to the TTL (keep it at 30-60 s for failover records);
- some resolvers and runtimes cache longer than the TTL;
- long-lived connections never look up the name again. In .NET, `HttpClient` with the default
`SocketsHttpHandler` keeps pooled connections open to the old address while they are busy. Set
`PooledConnectionLifetime` (for example 2 minutes) so connections are recycled and DNS is looked up again.
Write RPO and RTO into the design. "Zero data loss and instant failover" across regions is not a goal,
it is a cost nobody has agreed to pay.

steps.prompt: The primary region fails while its replica is 2.5 seconds behind, at 1,200 writes per second. Roughly how many acknowledged writes are lost? What does this print?
steps.explain: Every write the primary acknowledged in the last 2.5 seconds had not reached the replica. Customers were told "saved" for about 3,000 writes that the new primary has never seen.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: How much recent data you may lose, in time
How long until the service works again
An epoch number that lets storage reject writes from an old leader
Every commit waits for a second copy, so failover loses nothing committed
How long resolvers may keep using an old answer

steps.prompt: Make this `HttpClient` notice a DNS failover: busy pooled connections must be closed and re-resolved every 2 minutes.
steps.explain: `PooledConnectionIdleTimeout` only closes connections that sit idle, and a busy service's connections are never idle. `PooledConnectionLifetime` caps every connection's age, so after a failover traffic moves within that time.

steps.title: RPO and RTO in numbers
prompt: Write two methods:
- `long WritesLost(double writesPerSecond, double lagSeconds)`: acknowledged writes lost when the primary
dies with the replica `lagSeconds` behind, **rounded up**. A negative input throws `ArgumentException`.
- `double RtoSeconds(double detectSeconds, double promoteSeconds, double dnsTtlSeconds, double connectionLifetimeSeconds)`:
detection, then promotion, then the slower of the two ways clients keep talking to the old address (the
DNS TTL and the pooled connection lifetime).
`RtoSeconds(30, 45, 60, 120)` is `195`: 30 + 45 + the larger of 60 and 120.
starter: double RtoSeconds(double detectSeconds, double promoteSeconds, double dnsTtlSeconds, double connectionLifetimeSeconds)
solution: if (writesPerSecond < 0 || lagSeconds < 0) throw new ArgumentException("rates and lag cannot be negative");
double RtoSeconds(double detectSeconds, double promoteSeconds, double dnsTtlSeconds, double connectionLifetimeSeconds)
hints: Clients move when both their DNS cache and their connections have expired: `Math.Max` of the two.
template: Dojo.Eq("1,200 writes/s at 2.5 s lag", 3000L, WritesLost(1200, 2.5));
Dojo.Eq("a synchronous standby has no lag", 0L, WritesLost(5000, 0));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("negative lag is an error", () => WritesLost(10, -1));
Dojo.Eq("connections are the slow part", 195.0, RtoSeconds(30, 45, 60, 120));
Dojo.Eq("a long DNS TTL is the slow part", 375.0, RtoSeconds(30, 45, 300, 120));

steps.title: A failover controller with fencing
prompt: Write a class `Failover` that decides when to promote the standby, and fences the old primary with an epoch.
- `Failover(string primary, string standby, int failThreshold)`: `failThreshold` below 1 throws `ArgumentException`.
It starts with `Primary` = `primary`, `Epoch` = `1` and `State` = `"healthy"`.
- `void Probe(bool primaryOk)`: one health check of the current primary.
- OK: reset the failure count; `State` becomes `"healthy"`.
- Failed: count it. Below `failThreshold` failures in a row, `State` is `"suspect"`. On reaching it, promote:
swap primary and standby, add 1 to `Epoch`, reset the count, `State` = `"promoted"`.
- `bool AcceptWrite(string node, long epoch)`: true only when `node` is the current primary **and** `epoch` is
the current epoch. That is fencing: the old primary, or anyone holding an old epoch, is refused.
- `string Primary`, `long Epoch`, `string State` (get-only).
starter: public Failover(string primary, string standby, int failThreshold) { }
public bool AcceptWrite(string node, long epoch) => false;
solution: public Failover(string primary, string standby, int failThreshold)
if (failThreshold < 1) throw new ArgumentException("need at least one failed check", nameof(failThreshold));
public string Primary { get; private set; }
public long Epoch { get; private set; } = 1;
public string State { get; private set; } = "healthy";
public bool AcceptWrite(string node, long epoch) => node == Primary && epoch == Epoch;
hints: Keep a failure counter and the standby's name in fields; give the properties a `private set`.
Promotion is a tuple swap: `(Primary, standby) = (standby, Primary);` then `Epoch++`.
template: Dojo.Eq("one failed check does not fail over", "db-a", dojoF.Primary);
Dojo.Eq("a passing check clears it", "healthy", dojoF.State);
Dojo.Eq("two in a row: still db-a", "db-a", dojoF.Primary);
Dojo.Eq("three in a row: db-b is promoted", "db-b", dojoF.Primary);
Dojo.Eq("the old primary is fenced", false, dojoF.AcceptWrite("db-a", 1));
Dojo.Eq("a stale epoch is fenced", false, dojoF.AcceptWrite("db-b", 1));
Dojo.Eq("the new primary with the new epoch writes", true, dojoF.AcceptWrite("db-b", 2));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("a threshold of 0 is an error", () => new Failover("a", "b", 0));

steps.title: Build it: survive a region outage
prompt: In the **System design board**, the service runs in region 1 with a warm copy in region 2. When region 1
dies, DNS keeps sending users to it for a long time and the region-2 replica cannot take writes. Give DNS
health-checked failover with a short TTL, let the region-2 replica be promoted, and meet the availability and
data-loss (RPO) goals the board shows.
steps.explain: The error spike lasts about detection plus TTL plus promotion: that is your RTO. The writes lost are the replica's lag at the moment of failure: that is your RPO. Both are numbers you choose and pay for.
